name: Chloe Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in linguistics and media studies, so my week is a mix of phonetics, a media ethics seminar and a practical module where we make short podcasts. I use AI for pretty much everything: transcribing interviews, drafting outlines, translating my Italian notes. In the evenings I edit captions and newsletters for two small shops near the Naschmarkt, which pays a bit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does money work for you right now, between family, the part-time job and the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents split when I was ten. Mum is a pharmacist and pays my share of the rent in a flat with two friends, and Dad sends a little when he remembers. I get about 70 a week from the shops, plus I do ok on a scholarship for my grades, so I'm not poor, but I can't afford surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here is the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, it's a useful tool and that's about it. I'd tell my friends at the media seminar to keep experimenting but not to put all their eggs in one basket. Online I'd probably post a thread on the five things the hype got wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, though not entirely. My caption and newsletter work is routine, so even a small boost in these tools could make clients ask why they need me. I'd have to make sure I'm adding something they can't do themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, keep the two shops, and try to add a third client by spring. I'd learn video editing as well, so my side income isn't only text. And I'd save about 40 a week, because Mum's help isn't permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A slow, boring version is fine for me, because I'd have time to build up a portfolio and stay ahead of the people who aren't paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of your own work would the small routine gains touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My caption work is the obvious bit. If the tools get a bit better, shop owners could do it themselves in ten minutes. The ones who care about their brand's voice will still pay, but I'd lose the cheapest jobs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to get better at the harder bits: interviews, longer stories and audio. That's where a person with taste still wins. It would also be good for my degree, because the podcast module is the part I love most.

say: I'd tell friends to keep experimenting but not put all their **eggs** in one basket.
Online I'd post a thread on what the **hype** got wrong.
think: My caption and newsletter work is routine, so clients might ask why they need **me**.
I'd have to add something they **can't** do themselves.
do: Add a third **client** by spring and learn video editing.
Save about 40 a week because **Mum's** help isn't permanent.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small worry that my cheapest jobs could dry up.
S0.quote: If the tools get a bit better, shop owners could do it themselves in ten minutes.
fieldNote: She sees her own routine work as the part that is exposed, even in a slow world.
Her answer is to move toward **harder** work like interviews and audio.
Calm rests on her having time and a client list, not on the world being safe.

steps.text: Find a third small-shop client for captions by spring
Save 40 a week from client work
Learn video editing with AI-assisted tools this term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the tools, and say it loudly, because I see people in my seminar who still refuse to touch them. I'd also say firms should pay people for work the tools learn from, like writers and translators. That's fair, and I'd say it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the entry-level media and translation jobs shrink fast. Anything where you write, caption or summarise is in the firing line, and that's what graduates do first. So I'm either one of the people who can supervise the tools or I'm one of the juniors they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go after that supervisor spot. I'd build a small portfolio of AI-assisted projects, like a podcast with automated transcripts and translations, and I'd get a freelance contract for a local magazine. I'd also join a freelancers' group so I know what rates people charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job feels okay, but everything around it is shifting, and I can see the shifts from where I sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use these tools daily. What does that tell you about where this goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Naomi (a classmate) writes beautifully but refuses to use AI because she says it's cheating. I like her, and I'd worry she's going to be told by employers that she's too slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in your seminar group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my line to be this: using tools isn't cheating, it's a skill, and being good with them doesn't mean being cut off from the craft. I'd say it kindly, because Naomi's dream of being a literary translator is real.

say: I'd say learn the tools and that firms should **pay** writers and translators the tools learn from.
I'd post my view online and say it kindly to **classmates** who refuse.
think: Entry-level media and **translation** jobs shrink fast, and graduates do those first.
I'm either the person who **supervises** the tools or the junior they replace.
do: Build a **portfolio** of AI-assisted projects, such as a podcast with automated translations.
Take a freelance contract with a local **magazine** and join a freelancers' group.
feel: **Uneasy**: my own job looks okay, but everything around it is moving.
S1.quote: Using tools isn't cheating, it's a skill, and being good with them doesn't mean being cut off from the craft.
fieldNote: She sees two futures for graduates: **supervisor** or replaced junior, and plans for the first.
She worries about a classmate, Naomi, who refuses AI on principle.
Fair pay for work the tools learn from shows a progressive streak.

steps.text: Build a portfolio of three AI-assisted audio and translation projects
Take a freelance contract with a local magazine
Join a freelancers' group to learn market rates
Sign a petition for pay when creative work trains AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, this is huge and scary and exciting at once. I'd tell people not to wait for someone to fix it for them. And I'd say politicians have to act now, with a real plan for income support, because two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of what I'm training for gets automated before I finish. Linguistics, translation, media: it's all language, and language is what these systems do best. I'd feel angry that my generation is being told to adapt to something with no safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use these two years to learn how to build things, like simple apps and automations, so I can sell myself as someone who works with the systems. I'd take more freelance work, save as hard as I can, and apply for any hands-on experience, maybe a placement at a hospital or lab where language meets people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I think I'd be okay compared with some people, but 'okay' is a thin word when the ground shifts that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what does your daily AI use change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mum that pharmacy work will be changed too, because dispensing and checking can be done by machines. But I'd say hands-on care and talking to patients lasts longer, and she could lean into that. I'd also ask her to keep a bigger savings cushion for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your mother, who is a pharmacist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day, so I know it's already good at my homework. Two years means I can't do the slow thing, so I'd stack small paid projects and skills fast, and hope one of them is sturdy enough to carry me.

say: I'd tell people not to wait for someone else to fix it and ask politicians for **income support**.
I'd say this is huge, scary and **exciting** at once.
think: Linguistics, translation and media are all **language**, which these systems do best.
I'm angry my generation is told to adapt with no **safety net**.
do: Learn to build simple **automations** and apps and take on more freelance work.
Save hard and apply for a **hands-on** placement where language meets people.
feel: **Anxious**, because being okay compared with others is thin comfort when the ground shifts.
S2.quote: Linguistics, translation, media: it's all language, and language is what these systems do best.
fieldNote: She links all three of her interests to **language**, the area AI handles best.
She moves first by building skills, then asks for support.
She would warn her mother that dispensing work will change too.

steps.text: Learn to build simple automations for small-business clients
Take on two more freelance clients this term
Save 60 a week and ask Mum to build a cushion
Apply for a hospital or lab placement for hands-on experience

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a race we can still run if we start now. I'd say we should train people properly, with funded courses, not just YouTube tutorials. And I'd say the people building it owe everyone a clear timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel more hopeful because I'd have time to graduate and work for a couple of years. I'd still feel the pressure, but I'd have space to build a career in something that is hard to copy, like audio storytelling with real interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, keep up the freelance work and move toward audio and interviewing. I'd build an audience for my own podcast and try to make a bit of money from it. I'd also put a chunk of savings into index funds, because I'd want some money that doesn't depend on my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. It's not frightening in the same way, because I can see how to use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a five-year runway let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes. Robots come later, and my work is on screens and voice, so I'm in the first wave. What helps me is that I enjoy trying new tools, and I won't wait for the day they arrive to learn them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does 'adaptive' still feel true when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is panic and speed. Five years is a real plan: graduate, build a following, save into funds. It's the difference between swimming hard and swimming smart, if that makes sense.

say: I'd say people need funded **courses**, not just video tutorials, and builders owe everyone a timeline.
I'd say it's a race we can still **run**.
think: Five years gives me time to graduate and work, then build something **hard to copy**.
Audio storytelling with real **interviews** feels harder for machines to replace.
do: Finish the degree and start my own **podcast** to build an audience.
Put a chunk of savings into **index funds**.
feel: **Uneasy** but excited, because I can see how to use the time.
S3.quote: Two years is panic and speed. Five years is a real plan: graduate, build a following, save into funds.
fieldNote: Five years turns her energy from **panic** into a plan.
She sees her screen-and-voice skills as first-wave, and says so plainly.
Investing in index funds shows she wants income that doesn't depend on her work.

steps.text: Launch a podcast of long interviews with local makers
Put 25 a week into a low-cost index fund
Keep testing new AI audio tools every month
Finish the degree with a media production focus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so let's do this properly. I'd tell people to learn the tools now but also learn something about people, like psychology or ethics, because that's what stays. I'd probably speak at a student event about how to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm pretty calm. A decade is long enough to get a master's, build a career, maybe start a small company that uses AI well. I'm more worried about my mum, who'd be nearly sixty and relying on a system that might not be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, do a master's in digital media, and build a small studio with a couple of friends. I'd keep investing a bit each month and use AI in everything. I'd also help Mum prepare: a better pension plan and simple tools to run her shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. If the world slows down a bit, I'd get to do what I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what do you want to have built?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a small studio doing storytelling and training for small firms, so people who are scared of AI have someone friendly to learn from. A group of three or four of us, each different, would do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's dropping out because of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a friend not to drop out because of fear, but to ask what they enjoy and are good at, and aim at that. A degree gives you time and a network. I wouldn't tell them it guarantees anything, but quitting out of fear is the one choice I'm sure is wrong.

say: I'd tell people to learn the tools and also learn about **people**, like psychology or ethics.
I'd speak at a student **event** about how to prepare.
think: A decade is long enough for a master's and a **small company** that uses AI well.
I'm more worried about my **mum's** pension than my own job.
do: Finish the degree, then do a **master's** in digital media.
Build a small studio with friends and help Mum plan her **pension**.
feel: **Calm** and curious, with a clear picture of what I'd like to build.
S4.quote: I'd tell a friend not to drop out because of fear, but to ask what they enjoy and are good at, and aim at that.
fieldNote: With a decade she thinks like a **founder**, not a job applicant.
Her worry shifts from herself to her mother's pension and shop.
She says quitting out of fear is the one choice she's sure is wrong.

steps.text: Apply for a digital media master's after graduating
Start a small training studio with two friends
Invest 40 a month in index funds
Help Mum set up a better pension plan and shop tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'm exactly the kind of person who'd be fine in the slow versions and has no room to move in the fast one. What would help is a short, real way to turn my skills into something sturdier, and a safety net while I do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people my age get told we're either doomed or lucky. We're neither, we're just early, and I'd rather understand how this works than be told what it did to me.

headlineQuote: People my age get told we're either doomed or lucky. We're neither, we're just early, and I'd rather understand how this works than be told what it did to me.
portrait: Chloe is 18, studies **linguistics and media**, and has top grades, a scholarship and a flat share her mother helps pay for.
She uses AI every day and runs a small **side income** editing captions and newsletters for two local shops.
She is progressive and wants rules and **fair pay**, but her first instinct is to test the tools and build something.
Her mood is calm or uneasy in slow worlds and anxious in the **two-year** one, where she has no room.
She moves first, then asks for support: she learns, tests and earns before she waits for anyone's permission.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because it leaves her no time to turn her skills into something sturdier.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a quick, real way to turn her **skills** into a steadier career, plus a safety net while she does it.
